explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, because the king did summon the elders. But the text says he went up with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, as well as the priests and the prophets. It even adds “…all the people small and great…” That's a whole crowd, friend, and not a committee.

That's right, baker. The elders were summoned, but they didn't go up alone. Josiah, king of Judah, went up to the house of the LORD with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests and the prophets too. The text says “…all the people small and great…” That's a whole crowd, and not a committee.

Yes, he read it. In their hearing, he read all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. Not a summary and not the highlights. All the words, out loud, with everybody listening. Josiah doesn't skim the terms and conditions.

Copying is a fine thing to do with a book, but that's not what the text says here. It says that in their hearing he read all the words of the Book of the Covenant. The people heard every word of it, straight from the king.

Sealing is my whole job with a cookie box, friend, so I get the idea. But this book goes the opposite way. It was found in the house of the LORD, and Josiah read all of its words in the hearing of the people. Nothing about this moment was closed up.

explanations.answer: A covenant to follow the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD “…to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, decrees, and statutes with all his heart and all his soul…” Notice the words “…all his heart and all his soul…” That's a promise with nothing held back.

explanations.answer: A plan to rebuild the city walls
explanations.explanation: Walls are a fine project, but this verse never mentions them. Standing by the pillar, Josiah makes a covenant before the LORD to follow Him and keep His commandments, decrees and statutes. This moment is a promise made before the LORD, and it's about the words in the book.

explanations.answer: A vow to never go to war
explanations.explanation: No vow like that shows up here. The text says the king made a covenant before the LORD to follow Him and to keep His commandments, decrees and statutes. He also promised to carry out the words of the covenant written in the book. War isn't even in the room.

Josiah did make the covenant, but he wasn't standing there alone. The text says, “And all the people entered into the covenant.” They had just heard every word of the book read out, and they joined him. It was a promise the whole crowd made together.

You got it, baker. The king made the covenant by the pillar, and then the verse says, “And all the people entered into the covenant.” Josiah didn't keep it to himself or leave the crowd as spectators. They stepped into it with him.

explanations.answer: The articles made for Baal and Asherah
explanations.explanation: Right. Josiah commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests second in rank and the doorkeepers to remove from the temple of the LORD “…all the articles made for Baal, Asherah, and all the host of heaven.” Baal and Asherah were false gods, and their things had no business in the LORD's house. I think that was a LOT of stuff to carry out.

Doorkeepers are in the verse, so I see the mix-up. But the order isn't about money. Josiah commanded Hilkiah, the priests second in rank and the doorkeepers to remove the articles made for Baal, Asherah and all the host of heaven from the temple of the LORD. Those were idol things, not cash.

explanations.answer: The timber bought for the repairs
explanations.explanation: Timber is a sensible guess, since a temple gets a lot of fixing up. But the text says something else. Josiah commanded the priests and doorkeepers to remove all the articles made for Baal, Asherah and all the host of heaven. Those were the things that had to go out of the LORD's temple.

explanations.answer: Burning incense to the sun and moon
explanations.explanation: That's the one. These were idolatrous priests, ordained by the kings of Judah to burn incense on the high places. The text says they burned it “…to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the constellations, and to all the host of heaven.” Josiah did away with them.

Taxes would make a very different verse. The text says these priests were ordained by the kings of Judah to burn incense on the high places. They burned it to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the constellations and to all the host of heaven. Nobody there was holding a clipboard.

No soldiers in this verse, friend. These priests had been ordained by the kings of Judah to burn incense on the high places in the cities of Judah and all around Jerusalem. It was incense to Baal, the sun and moon, the constellations and all the host of heaven. Josiah did away with them.

explanations.answer: Burns it and grinds it to powder
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the verse is plain about it. Josiah “…burned it, ground it to powder, and threw its dust on the graves of the common people.” He didn't stop at one step. That's burning, grinding AND scattering, and I thought I was thorough when I sweep the counter twice.

explanations.answer: Buries it deep in the valley
explanations.explanation: Burying is what you do when you want something to rest, and nothing here rests. The text says Josiah burned the Asherah pole in the Kidron Valley and ground it to powder. Then he threw its dust on the graves of the common people. No shovel needed.

explanations.answer: Sends it back to its makers
explanations.explanation: No return to sender on this one, friend. The text says Josiah brought the Asherah pole out of the house of the LORD to the Kidron Valley. There he burned it and ground it to powder, and he threw its dust on the graves of the common people. Nothing was left to ship back.

That's the word. Josiah brought all the priests from the cities of Judah and desecrated the high places, from Geba to Beersheba, where the priests had burned incense. That's a long stretch of ground, from one end to the other. Josiah's reach was wide.

Restoring is the opposite of what the verse says. Josiah desecrated those high places, from Geba to Beersheba, where the priests had burned incense. That's a long trip, and I'd need a nap and a cookie break halfway. Nothing there got fixed up.

Guard duty would have meant keeping those places safe. The text says Josiah desecrated them instead. That was from Geba to Beersheba, wherever the priests had burned incense. They were not protected, friend.

Yes, that's what the verse says. The priests of the high places did not come up to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem. The text adds that they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests. I'll let that sit there without adding anything of my own.

The verse says the opposite, baker. The priests of the high places “…did not come up to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem…” The text goes on to say they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests. So the answer here is True.

explanations.answer: So no one could sacrifice a child to Molech
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Josiah desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom “…so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech.” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. The text shows Josiah closing that place down.

explanations.answer: So no army could camp in the valley
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, and it's a heavy one. Josiah desecrated Topheth so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech. Armies and camps aren't in the verse. I think this is a sad part of the story.

explanations.answer: So no one could build houses there
explanations.explanation: Houses aren't the concern in this verse. The text says Josiah desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech. I think that's one of the hardest lines in the chapter. Josiah's act was about stopping that.

I get why a king might want a chariot. But the text says Josiah removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, and then “…Josiah burned up the chariots of the sun.” They didn't go to his army. They went up in flames.

That's right. Josiah removed the horses dedicated to the sun from the entrance to the house of the LORD. Then he burned up the chariots of the sun. No parade, no inheritance, and no extra ride for his army.

Yes, that's the word. Josiah pulled down the altars on the roof near the upper chamber of Ahaz and the altars in the two courtyards of the house of the LORD. Then the verse says, “The king pulverized them there and threw their dust into the Kidron Valley.” They went from altars to dust.

Repairing is something I do to my mixer, and it's not what the verse says. Josiah pulled those altars down, then pulverized them there. He threw their dust into the Kidron Valley. There was no fixing on this job.

Guarding means keeping something safe, and that's not what happens here. The text shows Josiah pulling down those altars and pulverizing them. After that, he threw their dust into the Kidron Valley. Those altars were not being protected, friend.

Yes, it's right there in the text. Josiah desecrated the high places that “…King Solomon of Israel…” had built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom. That's three gods of three different nations, the Sidonians, the Moabites and the Ammonites. Solomon, king of Israel, had built them.

Ahab was a king of Israel too (1 Kings 16:29), so I see how he came to mind. But this verse names someone else. It says King Solomon of Israel built those high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom. The name is right there in the verse.

Saul was a king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), so the guess isn't far off. But the text names a different king for these high places. It says King Solomon of Israel built them for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom. Verse 13 gives the name.

Yes, that's what the verse says. Josiah smashed the sacred pillars to pieces and cut down the Asherah poles. Then he covered the sites with human bones. It's a heavy detail, and I'll leave it at that.

The verse says this happened, baker. Josiah smashed the sacred pillars to pieces and cut down the Asherah poles. Then he “…covered the sites with human bones.” It's a heavy detail, so the answer here is True.

The text doesn't say he left it. At Bethel, Josiah pulled down the altar and burned the high place. He ground it to powder and then burned the Asherah pole (2 Kings 23:15). The pole went into the fire.
That's right. At Bethel, Josiah pulled down the altar, burned the high place and ground it to powder. Then verse 15 says he “…burned the Asherah pole.” The pole did not stay standing.

explanations.answer: Burns them on the altar to defile it
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Josiah saw the tombs on the hillside, sent someone to take the bones out, and burned them on the altar to defile it. The verse says this was “…according to the word of the LORD proclaimed by the man of God who had foretold these things.” It's a heavy scene, but the text ties it to that word.

The verse never takes the bones to Jerusalem. Josiah sent someone to take the bones out of the tombs. Then he burned them on the altar to defile it, according to the word of the LORD proclaimed by the man of God. I think this is a hard scene to read.

That would be a gentle ending, but it's not the one the text gives. Josiah had the bones taken out of the tombs and burned on the altar to defile it. The verse says that was according to the word of the LORD proclaimed by the man of God. It's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: The man of God who came from Judah
explanations.explanation: Yes. The men of the city told Josiah, “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these things that you have done to the altar of Bethel.” That's the man who had foretold all of this. Josiah looked at a tomb and heard that its owner had seen it coming.

Jeroboam, the king of Israel, is in the chapter, but not at this tomb. Verse 15 says he set up the high place at Bethel and caused Israel to sin. The men of the city said this tomb belongs to the man of God who came from Judah. That's a different man entirely.

Samuel was a prophet in Israel (1 Samuel 3:20) with a home in Ramah (1 Samuel 7:17), so it's a natural guess. But he isn't in this scene. The men of the city said the tomb is of the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed what Josiah did to the altar of Bethel.

I understand the mix-up, since Josiah did have bones burned on the altar at Bethel. But when he heard whose tomb it was, he said, “Let him rest…” He also said, “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” So that tomb stayed as it was.

That's right, baker. Josiah said, “Let him rest…” and then, “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” So they left his bones undisturbed, along with those of the prophet who had come from Samaria. That tomb was spared.

explanations.answer: Removes them all just as at Bethel
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says, “Just as Josiah had done at Bethel, so also in the cities of Samaria he removed all the shrines of the high places…” Those shrines had been set up by the kings of Israel who had provoked the LORD to anger. He took out all of them.

explanations.answer: Leaves them standing for the people
explanations.explanation: Not a single shrine was spared. The text says that just as Josiah had done at Bethel, so also in the cities of Samaria he removed all the shrines of the high places. The kings of Israel had set them up and provoked the LORD to anger. None of them stayed.

explanations.answer: Hands them over to the priests
explanations.explanation: Nobody got a handover here, friend. The text says Josiah removed all the shrines of the high places in the cities of Samaria, just as he had at Bethel. Those shrines had been set up by the kings of Israel who had provoked the LORD to anger. They were removed, not handed off.
